extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, patent attorneys, inventors, and law students studying patent drafting and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on drafting and construing patent claims for combinations, machines, manufactures, compositions, designs, processes/arts, and improvements under U.S. patent law; explains what must be claimed, what is excluded, joinder rules, and limits imposed by the specification and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims control over Description
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the Description and Claims disagree, the Claims control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim language governs the patentee's exclusive right even if the description suggests otherwise; however parts shown in the Description to be essential should be understood even if not mentioned in the Claim (see Ex parte Richardson (1875)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts shown essential in Description are understood
rubrics_metrics.description: That parts shown in the Description to be essential to the invention must be understood, though not mentioned in the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification shows certain parts as essential, they will be treated as such for claim interpretation even if omitted from claim language (Ex parte Richardson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings may limit a Claim when referred to
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim may be limited by the drawings, where it describes the device only by letters referring to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that points to drawings (e.g., by reference letters) can be confined by those drawings (Ex parte Marsh (1872)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings cannot replace written Description
rubrics_metrics.description: That drawings cannot so far supply the place of a written Description that a Claim can be construed to cover matter shown only in the drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter appearing only in drawings, without adequate written description, will not be treated as part of the claim scope (Gunn v. Savage (1887)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations must be claimed as inventions by themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is the union of several elements under one co-operative law and must be claimed as an invention by itself, distinct from its elements and from their law of co-operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination cannot be adequately protected by claims directed only to individual elements, to all elements collectively under a different co-operative law, or to elements separately considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claim must include all essential characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a combination must include all its essential characteristics and embrace enough to produce a distinct and useful result, while being confined to the union the inventor has created and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must distinguish new from old (by disclaimer or omission), point out any novel arrangement if that is the invention, and avoid introducing non-essential features.

rubrics_metrics.name: New arrangement must be specifically pointed out
rubrics_metrics.description: If the real invention consists only in the new arrangement of an existing combination, the Claim must point out the new arrangement as the limit of its request for protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to point out the special construction or arrangement that constitutes novelty renders the claim too broad (Terry Clock Co. v. New Haven Clock Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essential features should not be introduced into combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Features not essential to the combination should not be introduced into the Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including non-essential elements makes them 'essential' for purposes of the patent and prevents the patentee later asserting they are unnecessary (Rapid Service Store R.R. Co. v. Taylor; Fay v. Cordesman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude unrelated portions of wider art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the new combination forms merely a part of some art or instrument of wider scope, other portions should not be mentioned unless necessary; when necessary, they should be disclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming the connecting mechanism to a principal invention unless necessary and coupled with an appropriate disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must embrace enough to produce a unitary result
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a combination must embrace enough to produce a distinct, definable, and unitary result, though not necessarily enough to produce the entire result aimed at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims for inoperative combinations are void; the claimed combination must be operative and produce the asserted result (Ex parte Rheutan; Torrant v. Duluth Lumber Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim invalid if it includes non-coacting element
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim including an element not co-acting as part of the combination is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that do not participate in the cooperative operation cannot properly be part of a combination claim (Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claim covers only the precise combination claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a combination covers the exact combination claimed and nothing more; it does not protect the elements, their mode of union, or their cooperative law separately considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It does not embrace other unions of the same elements with additional elements or different unions among subsets of those elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive terms ('means','mechanism') are improper in combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: That 'means,' 'mechanism,' and similar comprehensive terms are not proper in Claims for combinations for the purpose of pointing out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such broad catch-alls fail to identify the invention's inventive elements (Ex parte Paige; Ex parte Wilkin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words like 'substantially as described' are limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim for 'substantially as described' will be limited to the elements described as composing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases of generality do not enlarge a claim beyond the elements and mode of union set forth in the Description (Hailes v. Van Wormer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted elements are excluded from the claimed combination
rubrics_metrics.description: That elements omitted from the Claim are thereby excluded from the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed elements of a described combination are thereby typically conceded to be old as to that patent, though they may be reserved for later patents (Bowell v. Lindsay; Conover v. Roach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim for combination can be joined with claims for elements/sub-combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of a combination may contain several different Claims: besides the Claim for the combination as a whole, each of its elements and sub-combinations, if new and patentable, may also be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But claims for the same element performing different functions or for different combinations of the same elements cannot be inserted unless joinder rules permit (Pattee v. Moline Plow Co.; Ex parte Shepard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that make non-essential elements essential bind patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim including non-essential elements makes them essential, and the patentee cannot afterwards assert they are unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft carefully: including extra elements in a claim may change scope irrevocably (Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.; Boyer v. Schultz Belting Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for elements may be separately asserted though only useful in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: That the elements, if new, may be separately claimed even though useless out of the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate claims for new elements or sub-combinations are permitted when they are independently patentable (Stevens v. Pritchard; Henderson v. Cleveland Co-operative Stove Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different combinations of the same elements cannot be covered by one patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Different combinations of the same elements (particularly when performing different functions) cannot be covered by a single patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot claim multiple distinct combinations of the same components in one patent application (Ex parte Shepard; Ex parte Wheat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form flexibility of combination Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Any form of words may be employed in a Claim for a combination provided it accurately describes the real invention; enumerating elements and stating their method of combination is perfect but not always possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor lacks full understanding of modes of union, it suffices that he combined elements and produced a new operative means and that language makes invention intelligible to public so they can practise it and perceive claim limits (§526b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means claims limited to particular arrangement, not to function
rubrics_metrics.description: The means alone are claimed, and claimed only when specially arranged to produce a given result; this is far from claiming a function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to mere functions or results (without structural limitation) are improper; the specific means arranged to produce the effect must be described (Silsby v. Foote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (art) claims should enumerate essential acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for an art should enumerate the acts in which its essential character resides and set them forth to identify them with acts in the Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mode is left to inventor's discretion, but there is danger of departing from the Description. Claims for use of apparatus (versus claim for the art) should follow the nature of the Description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim use of a machine as an art unless distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: A Description relating to the production of an effect by the use of mechanism should conclude with a Claim for the machine only, not for the art of using it, unless its use for the purpose named is a distinct invention and has been described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, when a Description sets forth a new process, the Claim should be for the art only, not for the apparatus unless the apparatus itself is the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims cover all ways of practicing the art if stated generally
rubrics_metrics.description: An art covers all ways of practising it, and if its elements possess equivalents, a general Claim may cover it under every form; a specific Claim will cover the method as described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general process claim is broad; specific method claims protect particular implementations (Tilghman v. Proctor).

rubrics_metrics.name: A Claim for a process does not embrace the product
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim for a process does not embrace the product, although no other mode of producing it is yet discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process and product are distinct patentable subjects; claiming one typically does not confer rights over the other (Goodyear v. Wait; O'Reilly v. Morse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine must be claimed as a specific piece of mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine must be claimed as a specific piece of mechanism, not as a mode of operation, a principle, an idea, a means of producing an effect, or an effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New machine parts must be clearly pointed out and claimed; unclaimed or un-invented parts should not be mentioned or must be disclaimed. 'Means of doing' phrasing is improper (Ex parte Bates; Hatch v. Moffitt).

rubrics_metrics.name: In a machine patent, do not claim the mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: That in a machine patent a Claim for the 'mode of operation' is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should describe structural elements; asserting 'mode of operation' without structure will not sustain validity (Hatch v. Moffitt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture must be claimed as a new product distinct from process
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacture must be claimed as a new product, apart from any Claim for the process of making it or for the purpose for which it is employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product is new, enumerate essential qualities. If character depends on method of production, claim it only as produced by that specific process. 'Article of manufacture' has no special claim significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim for a manufacture should not set forth the process
rubrics_metrics.description: That a Claim for the manufacture should not explain nor set forth the process by which it is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims for the product should focus on product qualities; process descriptions belong in the specification and separate process claims if appropriate (Ex parte Shalters; Ex parte Cobb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims do not cover products made by subsequently discovered equivalent substances
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a product formed of certain described substances having certain qualities does not cover products formed of subsequently discovered substances having the same qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical/product claims are generally limited to the described substances or their equivalents as disclosed (Goodyear v. Berry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single composition requires single Claim and must enumerate ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: A single composition of matter requires only a single Claim, set forth by enumerating its elements and stating the mode of their union and the essential qualities of the resulting composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the composition consists of well-known ingredients, the Claim should enumerate them; if proportions/mode not stated, those in the Description are presumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims cover only same use of same or equivalent ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a chemical composition covers only the same use of the same or equivalent chemical ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to compositions are limited in scope to the uses and ingredient equivalents described (Goodyear v. Berry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Claim must be specific and confined to ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a design must be as distinct and specific as any other Claim and should mention nothing beyond the configuration or ornamentation constituting the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include qualities of the material or mechanical functions; Claims may be verbal descriptions or references to drawings and should contain 'as shown and described' to limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct designs cannot be joined in one Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Different designs cannot be embraced in a single Claim, and Claims for distinct designs cannot be joined unless they are so dependent on each other as to fit joinder rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate designs require separate claims (Ex parte Gerard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement claims must distinguish new from old
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is essentially distinct from the original art or instrument and a Claim for an improvement must define the improvement and fully and accurately distinguish it from the old invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should confine themselves entirely to the characteristics of the improvement, embracing nothing not necessarily connected; if original features are mentioned they must be clearly not claimed as new (Ex parte McMurray; Whitemore v. Cutter).
